A commander starts after his opponent. He takes the long road, the one the opponent is not watching. He arrives at the goal first. The opponent, who took the obvious route, spends the whole journey wondering how that happened.

Sun Tzu calls this the artifice of deviation. The circuitous route, taken by design, becomes the direct one. The apparent disadvantage of starting late dissolves when the opponent cannot see where you are going. The brilliant move is not the fastest path from here to there. It is the path the opponent left unguarded.

But the deviation has a cost when speed is forced. Sun Tzu is precise about this. A march of one hundred li with rolled-up armor strips out all the leaders. A march of fifty li leaves half the force behind. Even thirty li costs a third of the army. Speed is not free. The commander who demands too much from the march arrives at the goal diminished, or does not arrive at all.

Morale runs on a daily clock. Morning spirit is the keenest. By noon it is flagging. By evening it is spent. This is not metaphor. It is a tactical variable. A keen opponent is not the right opponent to attack. Wait them out. Attack when their spirit is in the afternoon or the evening. Your own morning strength is not just an asset for one battle. It is something to protect and time.

Gongs and drums carry the army's attention across distance. Banners and flags extend its sight. The whole force becomes one organism when these signals work. And seven rules close the chapter, each naming a specific trap that looks like an opportunity but is not.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
An order is given: boots are rolled up, the army marches through the night. By the time half the distance is covered, the force is a fraction of what it was. The leaders who stayed with the pace are the strongest; many of the rest have been swallowed by the distance. What arrives at the objective is not the force that set out.

Sun Tzu's forced-march schedule is not a caution about effort. It is a precise cost table. One hundred li at maximum speed loses all leaders. Fifty li loses half the force. Thirty li loses a third. The faster the march, the smaller the fraction that arrives. A commander who chooses the fastest route and arrives with one-tenth of the force has not saved time. He has converted an army into a reconnaissance element.

The deviation principle sits behind all of this. The long route is not the slow route when the opponent is watching the short one. Start after them, take the route they vacated, arrive before them. The paradox resolves when you understand that apparent distance is irrelevant if the opponent's attention is committed elsewhere.

Morale is a time resource with a daily cycle. Morning spirit is keenest. Attack a flagging opponent; wait out a keen one. The timing is not about psychology in the soft sense. It is a tactical calculation about when your force has the structural advantage over theirs.

Gongs and drums unify a dispersed force in noise. Banners and flags direct eyes across distance. Together they allow a large force to act as a single organism. And seven prohibitions name the specific traps a commander must recognize and refuse.

The mechanism has two simultaneous requirements. The lure must hold. The deviation route must be genuinely clear. If the lure is detected, the opponent has no reason to follow it. If the route is contested, the deviation is simply a longer path to the same resistance. Both requirements depend on intelligence the chapter identifies as necessary but does not specify how to obtain.

Forced march adds a second constraint. The cost schedule is specific: one hundred li loses all leaders, fifty li loses half the force, thirty li loses a third. This is a diminishing-returns claim about force integrity as march speed increases. A commander who selects the fastest available route but arrives with one-tenth of the planned force has produced a reconnaissance element, not an army. The deviation provides positional advantage; the march schedule determines whether sufficient force arrives to exploit it.

The three logistics dependencies, baggage, provisions, and supply bases, form a hierarchy in which losing any one converts the march into a sprint toward the limit of the army's effective range. Alliance knowledge, terrain knowledge, and local guides are listed as intelligence prerequisites that make movement reliable rather than reckless. The logistics section is simultaneously a planning framework and a map of the force's structural vulnerabilities.

Morale timing extends beyond the engagement itself. The daily cycle is the first axis: attack the flagging opponent, wait out the keen one. The situational variables add the rest: wait at ease while they toil, be fed while they are hungry, be near the goal while they are still far. These advantages compound. A force that has stacked all of them before the engagement begins has made the contest structurally unequal in its own favor.

Gongs and drums provide the signal system that makes unified action possible across distance and noise. Banners and flags extend visual coordination when voice cannot carry. Together they allow the commander to act as the mind of a large, dispersed organism.

Seven prohibitions close the chapter, each naming a specific trap by its surface appearance. Simulated flight looks like retreat. A keen opponent's temper looks like vulnerability. Bait troops look like weakness. In each case, the apparent opportunity contains a specific mechanism of danger. The prohibitions name the pattern without providing the method for identifying when a specific situation is an instance of it.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Sun Tzu's maneuvering chapter is a sequence of constraints on the deviation principle. Deviation is the thesis: start after the opponent, take the unguarded route, arrive first. Each subsequent argument in the chapter names a condition under which the deviation fails or becomes more expensive.

Forced march cost is the first constraint. The deviation is worthless if the force that arrives cannot accomplish the objective. The cost schedule is precise: one hundred li loses all leaders, fifty li loses half the force, thirty li loses a third. The structure of the loss matters as much as the quantity. Losing all leaders at one hundred li is not the same as losing half the rank and file at fifty. A leaderless force cannot execute coordinated action. The numbers describe the damage; the structure determines its operational effect.

Logistics is the second constraint. The deviation route must sustain the force not just to the objective but through the campaign. Baggage, provisions, and supply bases each represent a limit on how far and how long the force can operate. Each is also a lever the opponent can target. An opponent who cannot match the force in direct combat can cut its supply line and wait. The logistics section is both a planning guide and a vulnerability map.

Morale timing is the third constraint. Even a force that deviated successfully, arrived intact, and is logistically sustained must attack at the right moment. Morning spirit is the sharpest weapon. Evening is the vulnerability. The compounding variables, rest, food, proximity to the objective, multiply the morale advantage when they align. A force that deviates to an uncontested position but attacks at the wrong moment has wasted the positional advantage.

The seven prohibitions are the chapter's closing argument about the limits of any principle. Each names a situation where the surface appearance is an opportunity and the underlying structure is a trap. The prohibitions require exactly the situational judgment that the rules cannot provide. A commander who must decide whether to pursue a retreating force has precisely the uncertainty the prohibition is trying to address. The rule names what not to do. Knowing when the specific situation is an instance of the rule is the skill the prohibition points toward but cannot teach.

The route must be genuinely clear against conditions that may have changed since the intelligence was gathered. A sophisticated opponent who suspects a deviation will not follow the lure, which means the deviation advantage only materializes against opponents whose intelligence collection is weaker than the deviating commander's misdirection.

scenario.gentle: Hendrik is preparing to launch a new analytics product. Every major competitor in the category uses the same distribution route: enterprise sales teams reaching large company buyers through established procurement channels. It is the obvious path. It is also contested, expensive, and slow. Hendrik has identified a different route: specialty data consultancies that serve mid-market companies, a segment the category leaders have not cultivated and do not defend. The consultancy route takes longer to build. But the segment is uncontested.
scenario.direct: Hendrik is launching an analytics product into a category where the established distribution route is enterprise sales through large company procurement. Every competitor is on the same road, and the road is crowded. He has identified an alternative: partnership with specialty data consultancies serving mid-market companies, a segment the category leaders have not entered. The consultancy route takes months longer to develop than the direct enterprise channel. But when it arrives, it arrives at a position no competitor has prepared to defend.
scenario.competitive: Hendrik's new analytics product faces a launch choice. The direct route is enterprise sales through established procurement channels, the same road every major competitor is using. It is fast to start but immediately contested. The deviation route is specialty data consultancies serving mid-market buyers, a segment the category leaders have overlooked. The consultancy route takes longer to build and produces no visible momentum in the first quarter. The enterprise route produces immediate pipeline but lands the product in a position the competitors have already fortified.

examples.title: Hendrik Chooses the Deviation Route to Market

whatToDo.gentle: Hendrik takes the consultancy route. He spends the first quarter building relationships with twelve specialty firms, providing training, and developing a referral structure that does not require the consultancies to change their existing workflow. The work is slow and invisible. By the second quarter, the product is moving through consultancy channels into a segment where none of the category leaders have a presence. When the enterprise competitors notice the mid-market activity, Hendrik has already established relationships they would take months to replicate.
whatToDo.direct: Hendrik commits to the consultancy route and accepts the slower start. He builds the partnership program over the first quarter: onboarding, training, referral structure, technical support for consultancy staff. No revenue comes from this route in quarter one. In quarter two, deals begin closing through consultancy partners in the mid-market segment. By the time the enterprise competitors observe the activity, Hendrik has established a position they cannot quickly replicate without dismantling their existing enterprise-focused sales motion.
whatToDo.competitive: Hendrik takes the deviation route and absorbs the first-quarter delay. He builds the consultancy partnership program: twelve firms, structured referral incentives, technical enablement, co-marketing. No quarter-one revenue. In quarter two, the consultancy channel begins producing. In quarter three, it is the product's fastest-growing segment. The enterprise competitors are not present in the mid-market. Entering it now would require building the consultancy relationships Hendrik spent two quarters developing.

whyItMatters.gentle: The broader principle is that the most contested route is not always the most useful one. When every competitor takes the same obvious path, the path becomes crowded and expensive, and arriving on it later than the leaders does not produce a strong position. An uncontested route, even a longer one, arrives at a position that the obvious-route competitors are not prepared to defend. The deviation is not a shortcut. It is a choice about where to compete.
whyItMatters.direct: The broader principle is about what it means to arrive first. Hendrik did not arrive first on the enterprise route. He would have been seventh or eighth into a position the leaders already held. He arrived first on the consultancy route. First on an uncontested path is a stronger position than third or fourth on the obvious one, even if the obvious route would have produced earlier revenue. The deviation trades speed for position, and the trade is worth making when the obvious route leads to a position that is already occupied.
whyItMatters.competitive: The broader principle is that the deviation route is not slower. It is slower to the contested position and faster to the uncontested one. Hendrik's competitors reached the enterprise segment before him and will remain ahead there. He reached the mid-market consultancy segment before them and will be harder to displace there. The question is not which route is faster in absolute terms. It is which route arrives at a position worth holding.

scenario.gentle: Zara and Jomo are both enrolled in the same culinary school competition program. The competition runs three rounds over two days. Both teams have roughly equal technical skills. Zara's team pushes hard from the first round, going all-out on technique and presentation, winning both early rounds clearly. Jomo's team performs well but holds something back in the first two rounds, finishing second each time. By the third round, Zara's team is visibly flagging. Jomo's team delivers their best work of the competition in the final round.
scenario.direct: Zara and Jomo both enter a three-round culinary school competition with comparable technical skills. Zara's team treats each round as a maximum-effort event. They win rounds one and two clearly. By round three, the team is exhausted, and the quality of their work shows it. Jomo's team treats the first two rounds as accumulation phases, competing seriously but managing their energy and pacing their peak performance for the final round. Round three is the best work Jomo's team produces in the competition.
scenario.competitive: Zara's culinary team and Jomo's culinary team enter the same three-round school competition with equivalent skill sets. Zara's team goes to maximum effort in rounds one and two and holds the lead through both. Jomo's team finishes second in the early rounds while managing their energy deliberately. In round three, the gap inverts. Zara's team produces their worst work of the competition. Jomo's team produces their best. The team that conserved morning spirit for the final round outperformed the team that spent it early.

examples.title: Zara's Team Spends Morning Spirit Early; Jomo's Team Saves It for the Final Round

whatToDo.gentle: Jomo's team treats rounds one and two as contested but not total-effort events. They aim for a strong second-place finish in each, enough to stay in contention but not enough to require their full reserve. They identify which technical elements matter most in round three and save their sharpest focus for those elements. Zara's team does not make that distinction. Each round gets the same level of effort, which means round three gets whatever is left after rounds one and two.
whatToDo.direct: Jomo's team manages their energy deliberately across the three rounds. In rounds one and two, they perform at a level that keeps them in competition without requiring maximum output. They identify the scoring criteria with the highest weight in round three and reserve their sharpest execution for those criteria. Zara's team applies maximum effort uniformly, which means their round three performance is produced by whatever the team has left after two maximum-effort rounds.
whatToDo.competitive: Jomo's team identifies the round that matters most and manages their resources to peak there. In rounds one and two, they target second-place finishes at eighty percent capacity. In round three, they perform at full capacity against a Zara team running at sixty percent of their round-one level. Zara's team never made the distinction between which round deserved full effort and which rounds required only enough effort to stay in contention.

whyItMatters.gentle: Morale runs on a cycle in competition settings just as it does in any other high-stakes context. A team that spends its peak energy early will not have that energy for the final round. Jomo's team did not win by being more skilled. They won by managing when to spend their best. The question worth asking is whether your current approach to sustained competition treats energy as a fixed resource to be used evenly or as a time resource to be spent at the moment it produces the most value.
whyItMatters.direct: The self-directed question is whether your current competition preparation distinguishes between rounds or events that require maximum output and those that require only enough output to stay in contention. Jomo's team won because they treated morale as a time resource with a specific peak. Zara's team lost because they treated it as an inventory that could be refilled between rounds. Which assumption does your current preparation reflect?
whyItMatters.competitive: The question worth asking is whether your most important competitions are structured as maximum-effort events throughout, or whether you have identified which moments in a sustained competition require your peak and have built a resource management plan around that. Jomo's team beat a more conspicuously dominant team in round three not because of superior skill but because of superior timing. Is your competition strategy managing energy as a time resource or treating it as a renewable input?

scenario.gentle: Naomi has been trying to have a serious conversation with her father for months. The topic is a financial decision he made without consulting the family, and it has created real tension. Every time she has raised it, the conversation has collapsed. She has tried to start it after dinner. She has tried to bring it up on weekday evenings when he is tired from work. Each time, her father becomes defensive immediately, and the conversation ends before it begins. She has not yet tried the morning.
scenario.direct: Naomi needs to talk to her father about a financial decision that has affected the whole family. She has attempted the conversation four times, always in the evenings after he has finished work. Each attempt ends with him becoming defensive and the topic being dropped. The conversation she needs to have is not getting done because the timing is consistently wrong. She has all the information she needs. What she does not have is the right moment.
scenario.competitive: Naomi has tried to have the same conversation with her father four times. Same topic, same information, same outcome each time: defensiveness within ninety seconds and a dropped conversation. She has been trying in the evenings after work. She has identified the pattern and has not yet changed the approach.

examples.title: Naomi Waits for Saturday Morning to Have the Conversation That Failed Four Times

whatToDo.gentle: Naomi waits until a Saturday morning when her father is up before anyone else in the house. She sits down with him then, with coffee, before the day has made any demands on either of them. She starts the conversation not with the financial decision itself but with a smaller acknowledgment that she has been wanting to talk to him. He is more open than she expected. The conversation she could not have in any of four evening attempts takes place in twenty minutes on a Saturday morning.
whatToDo.direct: Naomi identifies Saturday morning as the structural opportunity. Her father is at his most open early in the day, before work demands or family activity has accumulated any pressure. She does not try to engineer the moment. She simply waits for a Saturday when he is up first and sits down with him before the morning fills in. She opens the conversation with the relational acknowledgment rather than the content, which gives him a reason to engage rather than defend. The conversation moves.
whatToDo.competitive: Naomi stops attempting the conversation in the evenings. She waits for a Saturday morning, positions herself in the kitchen before anyone else is up, and opens with a relational entry point rather than the disputed content. Her father's morning state is genuinely more open. The conversation that failed four times in the evenings takes twenty minutes on a Saturday morning and ends with a plan.

whyItMatters.gentle: The surprising implication is that the same conversation, with the same content, said by the same person to the same person, can produce a completely different outcome depending on when it happens. Naomi did not change her argument. She did not acquire new information. She changed the timing. The evening version of her father could not hear what she needed to say. The morning version could. Morale timing is not a manipulation strategy. It is a recognition that the person you are talking to is different at different points in the day, and so are you.
whyItMatters.direct: The surprising implication is that timing determines accessibility more than content does. Naomi's argument was the same in every attempt. Her father's capacity to hear it was not. The evening version of him was a defended, tired person. The morning version was genuinely more available. The conversation Naomi needed to have was always possible. It required the right timing to become actual. Content quality is often the wrong variable to optimize when a conversation keeps failing. Timing is usually the more tractable one.
whyItMatters.competitive: The surprising implication is that access is a function of timing, not just relationship. Naomi had the relationship and the argument in all four failed attempts. What she lacked was the right moment. Saturday morning was not strategically engineered. It was the natural state of the person she needed to reach. The morale-timing principle applied to personal relationships does not mean treating the other person as an adversary to be managed. It means recognizing that the person's capacity to engage is a variable, not a constant, and that timing a difficult conversation to their peak availability is both more effective and more respectful than forcing it when they cannot hear it.

scenario.gentle: Tomas and his colleague Celia are preparing to launch an internal initiative. The quarterly planning cycle closes in three weeks. If they launch before the cycle closes, their initiative will be on record before the agenda is set for the next quarter, and leadership will see it as an active project rather than a proposal. But launching in three weeks means launching without completing several important preparation steps. If they wait until after the cycle, they have time to prepare fully but arrive as a proposal competing for attention in a crowded agenda.
scenario.direct: Tomas and Celia are deciding when to launch an internal initiative. Launching before the quarterly planning cycle means arriving at the decision table as an active project, not a proposal, which carries more weight in how leadership responds. But launching before the cycle also means launching with incomplete preparation, which may create problems that damage the initiative's credibility. Waiting until after the cycle means full preparation but lower positioning in a crowded post-cycle agenda.
scenario.competitive: Tomas and Celia's initiative has a timing problem. Launching before the quarterly planning cycle closes positions it as an active project during the planning review. Launching after puts it in a crowded proposal field. The pre-cycle launch requires cutting preparation short. The post-cycle launch allows full preparation but costs the timing advantage. The question is whether the positional benefit of arriving before the cycle outweighs the credibility cost of incomplete preparation.

examples.title: Tomas and Celia Weigh Forced-March Cost Against Timing Advantage

whatToDo.gentle: Tomas and Celia map what incomplete preparation would actually cost. They identify three preparation steps they would cut if they launch in three weeks. Two of those steps can be completed in parallel with the early launch without damaging the initiative's initial credibility. One of them, a stakeholder alignment conversation, cannot wait and cannot be rushed. They do that one in the next ten days and launch the other preparation steps in parallel. They hit the pre-cycle window with the most critical preparation complete and the rest in progress.
whatToDo.direct: Tomas and Celia separate the preparation steps into those that are critical to credibility and those that can run in parallel with an early launch. The stakeholder alignment step is critical and cannot be rushed. Everything else can be built after launch without damaging the initiative's standing. They complete the stakeholder alignment immediately, launch the initiative ten days before the planning cycle, and continue preparation work in the post-launch period. They arrive before the cycle with the critical foundations in place.
whatToDo.competitive: Tomas and Celia audit their preparation checklist. They sort items by whether they are credibility-critical at launch or credibility-neutral. Credibility-critical items must be complete before launch. Credibility-neutral items can run in parallel. One item is both critical and time-consuming: stakeholder alignment. They prioritize that item exclusively for the next ten days, then launch. They hit the pre-cycle window with credibility intact and the remaining preparation running in parallel.

whyItMatters.gentle: The cross-domain application is that forced-march cost in organizational contexts works the same way it does in Sun Tzu's military argument. Launching with incomplete preparation is the equivalent of sending an army at one hundred li. Some of what you need to accomplish the objective arrives with you; some does not. The question is not whether to accept any forced-march cost. It is which cost is acceptable and which is disqualifying. Tomas and Celia did not eliminate the forced-march problem. They identified the one preparation step whose absence would disqualify the initiative and made sure it was complete before the march began.
whyItMatters.direct: The cross-domain application is that every organizational launch involves a forced-march cost when timing pressure is real. Launching before you are fully prepared means some fraction of your preparation does not arrive with the initiative. The question is which fraction. Tomas and Celia's approach is to distinguish the preparation that is load-bearing at launch from the preparation that can travel alongside it. That distinction does not eliminate the cost. It locates the cost where it is least damaging and avoids locating it where it would be disqualifying.
whyItMatters.competitive: The cross-domain principle is that forced-march cost in any timed-launch situation is about which preparation arrives and which does not. The competitive error is treating preparation as all-or-nothing: either wait for complete preparation and lose the timing window, or launch incomplete and accept the full credibility damage. Tomas and Celia's approach identifies the subset of preparation that is actually critical at the moment of launch and treats the rest as a parallel track. That distinction is available in any organizational context where timing pressure competes with preparation time.

scenario.gentle: Felix is the most technically skilled student in his culinary school cohort. In his first regional competition, he presents a menu built around a beef short rib dish with a specific sauce technique and a dessert using a method his instructor had never seen a student attempt before. He wins. The result is clear. His approach surprises the judges. The following semester, a second regional competition opens. Felix enters using the same menu, the same sauce technique, and the same dessert. His instructor warns him. Felix does not change the approach.
scenario.direct: Felix wins a regional culinary competition with a menu that contains a technical surprise: an unfamiliar sauce method and a dessert technique his judges have not seen in student competition. The surprise contributes materially to the result. In the following semester, Felix enters a second regional competition with the same menu. His instructor explicitly warns him that the competition field has been briefed on his first-competition approach and will have prepared counters. Felix does not modify the menu.
scenario.competitive: Felix wins a regional competition on the strength of technical execution and a menu that contains two genuine surprises. The following semester, he enters the same competition circuit with the same menu. His instructor warns him that a repeated menu gives the competition field a preparation map. Felix has the technical skill to compete. What he is submitting is not a menu. It is an advance briefing on his approach.

examples.title: Felix Repeats the Winning Menu and Loses the Element the Win Depended On

whatToDo.gentle: Felix should have treated his first competition win as a position that is now known, not as a method that is universally superior. The menu that won surprised the judges because they had not seen it before. Running the same menu in the following semester against judges who may have spoken to the previous judging panel and against competitors who have been told what to expect converts the surprise into a predictable approach. His instructor's warning was not about the quality of the menu. It was about what the menu no longer had that it had the first time.
whatToDo.direct: The preparation Felix needed to do was to identify which elements of the first menu produced the win and which of those elements depended on being unseen. The technical quality of the sauce and dessert is Felix's to keep. The surprise of those elements belongs to the first competition. Rebuilding the menu around a new element of unfamiliarity would have preserved the structural advantage of the win without presenting the competition field with a map of what to prepare against.
whatToDo.competitive: Felix's preparation for the second competition should have begun with the question of what, exactly, won the first one. Technical quality is transportable across competitions. Unfamiliarity is not. The winning menu was not superior because it was the menu Felix built. It was superior in part because the judges and competitors had not modeled it. Entering the same circuit with the same menu six months later is submitting a scouting report on yourself.

whyItMatters.gentle: The common trap is treating a successful tactic as permanently superior rather than as a tactic whose advantage was partly situational. Felix's menu was excellent. It was also new. Those two things produced the win together. Returning with the same menu kept the excellence but removed the newness. The competition field that had six months to study the previous result arrived prepared for exactly what Felix was presenting. A tactic that wins by surprise does not win by surprise the second time. This trap appears in any situation where a successful approach is repeated without asking whether part of its success was contextual.
whyItMatters.direct: The common trap is confusing the permanent quality of a tactic with the situational components of its success. Felix's sauce technique is permanently high quality. The judges' unfamiliarity with it was a situational component that existed only in the first competition. Repeating the menu preserved the quality and eliminated the situational component. The result was a technically excellent submission that the competition field had prepared for and could counter. Any field where competitive advantage depends partly on being unseen follows the same pattern: the advantage does not automatically travel with the tactic to the next contest.
whyItMatters.competitive: The common trap is repeating a successful approach without auditing which parts of the success are durable and which parts are consumed by the first use. Felix's technical skill is durable. The judging field's unfamiliarity with his sauce method was consumed in the first competition. A competitor who prepares for Felix by studying the previous result can neutralize the part of the advantage that depended on being unseen. This trap appears in any competitive context where some fraction of the first-contest advantage is positional or situational rather than intrinsic to the tactic itself.

scenario.gentle: Vera has been in a low-grade dispute with a neighbor for months over a shared fence that needs repair. Neither of them has initiated the direct conversation. Vera has been waiting for the right moment. She has been tracking the neighbor's patterns, trying to identify when they seem least defensive. She has a clear sense of when the neighbor is rushed, tired, or distracted, and she has been avoiding those windows. She has been building a mental model of when the neighbor is most available to hear her.
scenario.direct: Vera has been trying to raise a fence repair issue with a neighbor for three months without finding the right moment. She has been observing the neighbor's daily and weekly patterns, building a model of when they are most accessible versus most defended. She has identified several good windows and not used any of them. The reason, which she has not yet examined directly, is that her own availability to have the conversation has not been considered.
scenario.competitive: Vera has been waiting three months for the right moment to approach her neighbor about a fence dispute. She has been optimizing the timing entirely around the neighbor's state: studying their patterns, identifying low-defensiveness windows, avoiding high-friction moments. She has a good model of when the neighbor is most available. She has no model of her own availability. She has not raised the issue yet.

examples.title: Vera Realizes the Timing Principle Applies to Both Sides of the Conversation

whatToDo.gentle: Vera examines her own state before the next available window with the neighbor. She asks when she herself is most composed, most patient, and least likely to escalate if the neighbor responds defensively. She finds that her own peak is not always aligned with the neighbor's. The first time both windows overlap, she initiates the conversation. She discovers that preparing for her own state was as important as reading the neighbor's.
whatToDo.direct: Vera adds a second assessment to her timing model. She maps not only when the neighbor is most available but when she herself is most capable of handling defensiveness without escalating. She is composure: calm, patient, genuinely open to a resolution that is not entirely on her terms. The first window where both conditions are present, she initiates. The conversation goes better than any of the previous attempts she has imagined but not made.
whatToDo.competitive: Vera builds a two-sided timing model. One axis is the neighbor's state: availability, composure, lack of ongoing friction. The other axis is her own state: patience, composure, genuine orientation toward resolution. She has been optimizing one axis and ignoring the other. The first time both axes align, she initiates the conversation. She discovers that the two-sided model was more accurate than the one-sided model she had been running.

whyItMatters.gentle: The perspective reframe is that morale timing applies to both sides of any interaction, not just the side you are trying to influence. Vera had been treating the timing problem as a question about the neighbor's readiness. The neighbor's readiness is real and relevant. But Vera's own readiness determines how she handles resistance, how she responds to an initial defensive reaction, and whether the conversation moves toward resolution or collapses. The timing principle is bilateral. Applying it to only one side is half the model.
whyItMatters.direct: The perspective reframe is that the morale-timing principle is not a technique for reading other people. It is a framework for reading both parties to any interaction. Vera's model was accurate as far as it went. The neighbor's state is a real variable. But the commander who attacks when the opponent is flagging must also be able to sustain the engagement when the opponent's state turns. Vera's own composure under resistance is the variable that determines whether a good opening moment converts into a productive conversation or a stalled one.
whyItMatters.competitive: The perspective reframe is that a timing model that optimizes only the opponent's state is missing the variable that determines whether a good entry moment actually produces a good outcome. Vera had a sophisticated model of the neighbor's availability and zero model of her own. The best moment to approach an opponent is the intersection of their low-defensiveness and your high-composure, not simply their low-defensiveness alone. Morale timing applied to one side only is an incomplete version of the principle.

coreSkill.gentle: Reading the timing of your most important moves, identifying whether the current moment favors the direct route or a deviation, and whether morale conditions favor acting now or waiting.
coreSkill.direct: Assessing whether the most obvious route to a goal is the most contested one, and whether a less watched deviation route is available. Simultaneously reading the morale state of the people involved to determine whether the timing favors acting now or waiting.
coreSkill.competitive: Diagnosing in real time whether the direct route is best or whether a deviation route would arrive at a less contested position, while also assessing the forced-march cost of each route and the morale state of both sides before committing to a timing.

plan.gentle: If I am about to launch an initiative, I will assess whether the most obvious route is also the most contested and whether a deviation route exists that would arrive at a less defended position.
plan.direct: If I am about to launch an initiative, I will map the direct route and any available deviation route, assess the forced-march cost of each, and determine whether the timing advantage of the faster route outweighs the cost in preparation or force integrity.
plan.competitive: If I am about to launch an initiative, I will assess the direct route's contested state, map the available deviation routes, calculate the forced-march cost of each, and read the morale state of the key stakeholders before committing to a timing.

plan.gentle: If I am preparing for a high-stakes academic event, I will identify what the equivalent of a deviation looks like for my specific preparation and whether there is a less obvious preparation approach that competitors are not building.
plan.direct: If I am preparing for a high-stakes academic event, I will identify which rounds or moments in the event require maximum output and which require only enough output to stay in contention, and build my energy management around that distinction.
plan.competitive: If I am preparing for a high-stakes academic competition, I will map the preparation moves that competitors are making, identify the preparation angle they are not pursuing, and assess whether that angle can be developed within the available timeline at an acceptable cost.

plan.gentle: If I am timing a difficult conversation, I will assess the other person's current state and wait for the morning rather than the evening, and also check my own state before initiating.
plan.direct: If I am about to initiate a difficult conversation, I will assess both the other person's availability and my own composure before choosing the moment, and delay if either condition is not met.
plan.competitive: If I am timing a difficult conversation or confrontation, I will build a two-sided timing model: the other person's low-defensiveness state and my own high-composure state, and initiate only when both conditions are present simultaneously.

twentyFourHourChallenge.gentle: In the next 24 hours, identify one upcoming move and assess whether you are taking the direct route because it is actually best or because it is the most obvious.
twentyFourHourChallenge.direct: In the next 24 hours, identify one upcoming move and map both the direct route and any available deviation route. For each route, name the forced-march cost and the positional outcome. Then decide which route actually produces the better arrival.
twentyFourHourChallenge.competitive: In the next 24 hours, identify your most important upcoming move. Map the direct route, the deviation route, the forced-march cost of each, and the morale state of the people involved. Identify which combination of route and timing produces the most favorable arrival conditions.

weeklyPractice.gentle: Weekly, review your biggest planned moves for the coming week. For each one, ask: what is the obvious route, and is there a less contested one? What is the morale state of the people involved?
weeklyPractice.direct: Weekly, review your three most important planned moves. For each: identify the direct route and any deviation route, assess the forced-march cost of each, and read the morale state of the people involved. Determine whether the timing and route you have chosen actually produces the best arrival.
weeklyPractice.competitive: Weekly, review your three highest-stakes planned moves. For each: map direct and deviation routes, calculate forced-march cost, assess morale state of all parties, and identify any situations that match the seven-prohibitions pattern where the apparent opportunity may be the trap. Adjust timing and route choices before committing.

keyTakeawayCard.gentle: Sun Tzu says maneuver is the hardest part of war because it requires turning the long way around into the direct route, starting after the opponent and arriving first. But speed costs precisely: force-marching 100 li loses all your leaders, 50 li loses half your force, 30 li loses a third. Logistics must hold throughout. Morale has a daily clock: attack when the opponent is flagging, not when they are keen. And seven prohibitions name the traps that look like opportunities: the retreating enemy that is baiting you, the keen opponent who wants you to move first.
keyTakeawayCard.direct: Deviation is the art of taking the unexpected route and arriving at the goal before the opponent who took the obvious one. But speed has a precise cost: the forced-march schedule is a diminishing-returns claim, not a general caution. Logistics, baggage, provisions, supply bases, are not optional prerequisites. Morale is a time resource with a daily cycle; the chapter names when to attack and when to wait. The seven prohibitions close with the traps: situations that look like opportunities but carry a specific danger the prohibition names.
keyTakeawayCard.competitive: The deviation principle is the hardest to execute and the most valuable when it works: start later, arrive first, take the route no one was watching. The cost schedule is precise, know what you are trading when you trade it. Logistics is not support; it is the enabling condition for every other move. Morale timing is a real tactical variable: attack the evening army, not the morning one. And the seven prohibitions are not about restraint, they are about recognizing the difference between an opportunity and a trap.

questions.prompt: In Chapter 7 of The Art of War, what term does Sun Tzu use to describe the core strategic principle of turning a longer, indirect route into the faster, decisive path?
choices: A) The deviation principle
B) The supply doctrine
C) The morale cycle

explanation.gentle: Nice catch. The deviation principle is Sun Tzu's name for the maneuver in which a lure draws the enemy off the direct road, leaving that road open for you — so the roundabout way becomes the swift one.
explanation.direct: Sun Tzu's Chapter 7 opens with the deviation principle as the chapter's organizing concept: use misdirection (a working lure) to clear the direct path. Supply doctrine and morale cycle are real chapter topics but are not the named strategic principle.
explanation.competitive: B) The supply doctrine describes logistics prerequisites, not the principle of indirect-to-direct conversion. C) The morale cycle is the dawn-noon-dusk energy framework. Neither names the circuitous-becomes-direct maneuver that Sun Tzu explicitly calls the core difficulty of maneuvering.

questions.prompt: Sun Tzu describes a 'forced-march cost schedule' for covering 100 li to seize an advantage. Which outcome does he predict?
choices: A) The full army arrives intact but exhausted and fights at half effectiveness
B) Only the fastest tenth of the force arrives; the generals of the three divisions are captured
C) Two-thirds of the force arrives; the remainder catches up by nightfall

explanation.gentle: Nice catch. At 100 li, Sun Tzu says only the fastest tenth of the troops will arrive — the bulk of the force is strung out along the road — and the leaders of the three divisions will likely fall into enemy hands.
explanation.direct: Sun Tzu provides a precise diminishing-returns schedule: 100 li = only the top 10% arrive (generals captured); 50 li = two-thirds arrive; 30 li = full force intact. Choice C describes the 50-li outcome, not the 100-li outcome.
explanation.competitive: A) Sun Tzu does not describe the full army arriving at 100 li — the chapter explicitly states that most soldiers are left behind at that distance. C) Two-thirds arriving is the prediction for a 50-li forced march, not 100 li. Confusing the distances inverts the cost schedule.

questions.prompt: According to Sun Tzu's morale timing principle, when is the ideal moment to attack an enemy force?
choices: A) At dawn, when the enemy's morning spirit is at its keenest
B) At noon, when the enemy transitions between shifts of guard
C) In the evening, when the enemy's spirit is spent and its soldiers think only of home

explanation.gentle: Nice catch. Sun Tzu's daily morale cycle is explicit: morning spirit is keenest, noon it flags, evening it is spent. You wait until the opponent is at the bottom of that curve before you engage.
explanation.direct: The morale timing principle prescribes attacking during decline, not peak. Morning is when you should avoid engaging a fresh, spirited enemy; evening is when that same force is depleted. Choice A describes exactly the moment Sun Tzu says to withhold attack.
explanation.competitive: A) Attacking at dawn hits the enemy at peak morale — the opposite of Sun Tzu's advice. The text says 'avoid' keen morning spirit, not exploit it. B) Noon is the flagging midpoint, which Sun Tzu mentions but does not identify as the optimal strike moment; evening exhaustion is the preferred window.

questions.prompt: Amara is a project lead at a software consultancy competing for a lucrative enterprise contract. Her rival firm is pursuing the same client aggressively. Amara quietly arranges a flashy joint workshop with a secondary client — generating buzz that pulls her rival's attention and resources there. Meanwhile, Amara moves quickly to close the enterprise deal uncontested. Which element of Sun Tzu's deviation principle does Amara's plan depend on most critically?
choices: A) A large headcount advantage so she can pursue both opportunities simultaneously
B) A lure compelling enough that the rival genuinely redirects effort, combined with a clear path Amara can actually exploit
C) Perfect secrecy so the rival never learns about the enterprise contract

explanation.gentle: Nice catch. Sun Tzu's deviation principle requires two things working together: a lure that actually draws the opponent away, and a route that becomes genuinely available once they leave. Amara's plan hinges on both — the workshop lure must work AND the enterprise path must be clear.
explanation.direct: The deviation principle is not about secrecy alone or numerical superiority — it is a two-part mechanism: (1) a working lure that redirects the opponent and (2) a route that becomes passable as a result. If either part fails, the maneuver collapses. Amara's success depends entirely on this dual condition being met.
explanation.competitive: A) Headcount would enable parallel pursuit, which is not the deviation principle — it is just resource multiplication. Sun Tzu's insight is doing more with the same force by redirecting the opponent. C) Secrecy helps but is not the critical dependency; even if the rival learns of the enterprise contract after being fully committed to the workshop, the deviation has already worked. The lure's effectiveness and the route's accessibility are the load-bearing elements.

questions.prompt: Diego is a sales director at a B2B manufacturing firm. His team is behind on quota and he considers having every rep sprint to close as many deals as possible before month-end, accepting any terms to hit the number. He has seen the risk: reps burning out, margin destroyed, and key accounts poorly onboarded. Which of Sun Tzu's concepts from Chapter 7 most directly predicts Diego's problem if he proceeds?
choices: A) The seven prohibitions — specifically, do not pursue simulated flight
B) The forced-march cost schedule — speed traded for capability leaves only the fastest fraction functional
C) The logistics prerequisite — foraging from the enemy is necessary when supply lines are long

explanation.gentle: Nice catch. Sun Tzu's forced-march cost schedule maps directly onto Diego's situation: when you demand maximum speed over a fixed distance (or deadline), only the hardiest fraction of your force arrives intact. Most of the team — and most deal quality — is left strung out behind.
explanation.direct: The forced-march cost schedule is a diminishing-returns model: speed extracts a capability price. Diego's plan to sprint every rep to close at any cost mirrors the 100-li march — perhaps 10% of reps close strong deals, the rest burn out or produce low-margin, high-churn accounts. The chapter's cost schedule quantifies this trade-off precisely.
explanation.competitive: A) The seven prohibitions address trap-recognition in adversarial maneuver — Diego's problem is internal resource degradation, not falling for an enemy feint. C) The logistics prerequisite is about supply-chain dependency, not about the internal cost of forcing a team beyond sustainable pace. Only the forced-march cost schedule names the specific trade-off Diego is about to make.

questions.prompt: Yuki is a department head at a regional hospital. A competing hospital has just announced a new specialist service and patients are shifting over. Yuki's administrator pressures her to immediately launch a counter-program to stop the outflow. Yuki instead argues for waiting three months to staff properly, stockpile supplies, and train frontline teams before going public. Which pair of Sun Tzu's principles from Chapter 7 most directly supports Yuki's argument?
choices: A) Logistics prerequisites and morale timing — a force without supply cannot maneuver, and a rested, prepared force fights from a stronger morale position
B) The deviation principle and the seven prohibitions — lure the rival into overextension and avoid pursuing their feigned retreat
C) The forced-march cost schedule and the deviation principle — slow the march to preserve capability, then use a lure to draw patients back

explanation.gentle: Nice catch. Sun Tzu insists that an army without supply cannot maneuver effectively, and that morale timing — stacking rest, supply, and proximity before engaging — is the structural advantage that makes an attack decisive rather than desperate. Yuki is building exactly that stack.
explanation.direct: Yuki's argument rests on two Chapter 7 pillars: (1) logistics prerequisites — launch without proper staffing and supply and you cannot sustain the program; (2) morale timing — her team, fully trained and rested, will outperform a rushed, undersupplied launch. The three-month pause is Sun Tzu's 'await the order and calm' applied to a healthcare context.
explanation.competitive: B) The deviation principle and seven prohibitions concern adversarial maneuvering and trap recognition — useful in competitive strategy but not the argument Yuki is making, which is about internal readiness, not about luring a rival. C) The forced-march cost schedule does support slowing down, but the deviation principle requires a lure redirecting the rival, which Yuki's plan does not involve. The logistics plus morale pairing is the tightest fit.

questions.prompt: Sun Tzu warns against 'swallowing offered bait' as one of his seven prohibitions. What is the underlying structural reason this prohibition exists, and how does it connect to the deviation principle?
choices: A) Bait depletes your supply faster than direct assault, making the logistics situation untenable
B) Pursuing bait always violates morale timing because the enemy sets the bait at dawn when your troops are keenest and most likely to charge
C) The offered bait is itself the lure in a deviation maneuver — the opponent has constructed a trap where the apparent prize draws you off your position and onto ground of their choosing

explanation.gentle: Nice catch. The prohibition against swallowing bait is the deviation principle seen from the defender's perspective: the bait is the lure, and chasing it surrenders the position or route the opponent actually wants to clear. Recognizing bait means recognizing that you are being maneuvered against.
explanation.direct: The seven prohibitions are a trap-recognition framework. Each named trap has a surface appearance (fleeing soldiers, offered supplies) that invites a predictable response. 'Offered bait' is structurally identical to a lure in the deviation principle — the opponent is using it to move you so they can exploit the space you vacate. Understanding the prohibition requires understanding that the bait is not the objective; it is the mechanism.
explanation.competitive: A) The supply concern is real but is not why the prohibition exists — the prohibition is about positional and strategic manipulation, not logistics cost. B) There is no textual basis for the claim that bait is specifically set at dawn; the morale cycle operates independently of the bait prohibition. Conflating the two mechanisms misreads both.

questions.prompt: Sun Tzu states that an army without supplies, provisions, and base support 'cannot even start' a campaign. How does this logistics prerequisite interact with the deviation principle's requirement for a 'clear deviation route'?
choices: A) They are independent requirements; logistics determine whether you can fight at all, while deviation routes determine how you get there — both must be satisfied before maneuvering is viable
B) A strong logistics position makes the deviation principle unnecessary, because a well-supplied army can simply overpower the enemy on any route
C) The deviation principle compensates for logistics shortfalls by shortening the actual travel distance through misdirection

explanation.gentle: Nice catch. Sun Tzu treats logistics and the deviation route as separate but equally necessary conditions. An army with a perfect deviation plan and no supply will collapse on the route; an army with full supply and no viable deviation route will be contested the whole way. Both conditions must hold simultaneously.
explanation.direct: Chapter 7 integrates logistics and maneuvering as co-requisites, not substitutes. Logistics set the floor (without supply, no campaign is possible). The deviation principle sets the route strategy (how to arrive with force intact). Neither compensates for the absence of the other; both are prerequisites to effective maneuvering.
explanation.competitive: B) Sun Tzu never argues that supply replaces strategic ingenuity. Overwhelming supply does not eliminate the need for correct route strategy — an army marching directly into a contested route still takes casualties and loses the element of surprise regardless of provisioning. C) The deviation principle does not shorten travel distance — it makes a longer route strategically equivalent to a shorter one by clearing the obstacle. It does not reduce supply consumption; it potentially increases it on the longer path.

questions.prompt: A critic argues that Sun Tzu's seven prohibitions are too rigid: 'Real battles are chaotic — sometimes you must pursue retreating troops to prevent regrouping, even if it looks like simulated flight.' Evaluate this critique against the chapter's logic.
choices: A) The critique is partially valid: the prohibition against pursuit applies only to infantry engagements and Sun Tzu acknowledges cavalry commanders may pursue freely
B) The critique is valid; Sun Tzu's prohibitions are absolute rules that fail in fluid situations where regrouping is the greater threat
C) The critique misreads the prohibitions as mechanical bans rather than as a trap-recognition framework requiring the commander to distinguish genuine retreat from feigned retreat before acting

explanation.gentle: Nice catch. The seven prohibitions are not unconditional stop signs — they are a framework for recognizing the difference between a genuine situation and a manufactured appearance. The skill Sun Tzu is cultivating is discriminating judgment, not reflexive restraint. A commander who can reliably identify simulated flight is free to pursue genuine flight.
explanation.direct: The prohibitions are structured as 'do not X when X is a trap' — not 'never X.' The chapter's logic is that each prohibited action names a surface appearance (retreating soldiers, offered bait, a homeward army) that commonly conceals a trap. The competent commander learns to read the appearance accurately. The critic's objection assumes the prohibition bans pursuit categorically, which the text does not support.
explanation.competitive: A) There is no cavalry exception in Chapter 7 or elsewhere in the Giles translation; this choice fabricates a textual distinction that does not exist. B) Treating the prohibitions as rigid absolutes is the error the critic projects onto Sun Tzu, not a feature of the text. Sun Tzu is a strategist who repeatedly emphasizes situational reading over fixed rules — the prohibitions are taught as heuristics that require interpretation.

questions.prompt: Across Chapter 7, Sun Tzu argues that maneuvering — not direct confrontation — is the decisive advantage. Evaluate which of the following best captures the chapter's integrated claim about why maneuvering is superior.
choices: A) Maneuvering is superior because it conserves troops: by avoiding battle entirely, losses are minimized and the army remains intact for future engagements

B) Maneuvering converts multiple structural advantages simultaneously — route control, morale timing, logistics stability, and trap avoidance — into a compounding positional edge before a blow is struck
C) Maneuvering is superior primarily because speed of movement prevents the enemy from reacting, making the quality of the force less important than its velocity

explanation.gentle: Nice catch. Chapter 7's integrated argument is that maneuvering stacks multiple independent advantages — the deviation route clears the path, logistics ensure the force is functional on arrival, morale timing ensures the army is fresh and the enemy is spent, and trap-recognition prevents being diverted. These compound before engagement begins, which is why Sun Tzu treats maneuvering as the decisive act.
explanation.direct: The chapter is not a single-thesis argument about speed or casualty avoidance — it is a multi-factor framework. Deviation, logistics, morale timing, and the seven prohibitions are distinct mechanisms that reinforce each other. The integrated claim is that a commander who stacks all four arrives at the engagement already holding the decisive margin. No single mechanism captures this; the compounding is the point.
explanation.competitive: A) The chapter does not argue for avoiding battle — Sun Tzu elsewhere accepts that battle is sometimes necessary. Chapter 7 is about arriving at battle in the strongest possible position, not about bypassing it. C) Speed is explicitly shown to carry costs in the forced-march schedule — Sun Tzu cautions against prioritizing velocity above all else. Quality of force (intact supply, rested morale) is precisely what the chapter works to preserve against the temptation of pure speed.

back.gentle: Taking the long, unexpected route to arrive at the goal before the opponent who took the obvious path. The deviation works by using a lure to hold the opponent's attention on the wrong road while the deviating commander takes the route they have vacated. The long route becomes the direct one when the opponent's attention is committed elsewhere.
back.direct: The artifice of deviation turns the circuitous route into the direct one by enticing the opponent away from the real destination while taking the route they vacated. The mechanism requires both a working lure and a genuinely clear deviation route. When the lure fails to draw, or the deviation route is contested, the maneuver extends exposure without capturing the positional gain it was designed to produce.
back.competitive: The deviation converts the circuitous route into the direct one by exploiting an asymmetry in the opponent's intelligence. The mechanism requires that the lure hold the opponent's attention on the wrong route and that the deviation route be genuinely clear. Against a sophisticated opponent who detects the lure, the deviation reverses into a simple delay.

front.gentle: What does the 'artifice of deviation' mean?
front.direct: State the mechanism of the deviation principle and name the two conditions required for it to produce a timing advantage.
front.competitive: Explain the artifice of deviation and state the intelligence condition it requires that the chapter does not guarantee.

back.gentle: Morning spirit is keenest; it flags by noon; by evening it is spent. Attack when the opponent's spirit is flagging; wait when it is keen. The principle extends to all situational advantages: rest versus fatigue, fed versus hungry, near the goal versus far from it.
back.direct: The morale cycle runs from keen to flagging to spent across a single day. Act when the opponent is in the latter two phases; hold when they are in the first. The broader principle is compounding situational advantages: a rested, fed, near-the-goal force attacking an exhausted, hungry, distant one has made the engagement structurally unequal before the first move.
back.competitive: Morning spirit is keenest; noon it flags; evening it is spent. The tactical application is to attack when the opponent's cycle is down and wait when it is up. The harder implication is that applying the principle correctly requires accurate real-time intelligence about the opponent's actual state, not just their apparent one.

front.gentle: What does Sun Tzu say about morale timing?
front.direct: State the morale clock and explain the broader compounding principle it is part of.
front.competitive: State the morale-timing principle and name the intelligence problem that limits its application.

back.gentle: The forced-march cost of launching early is real: incomplete preparation, likely errors, and leadership awareness of gaps. But if the deviation route of launching before the planning cycle arrives at a position that would be contested or crowded after the cycle, the cost may be worth accepting. The question is whether the timing advantage opens a position that could not be claimed after the cycle, or whether arriving second but fully prepared would actually produce a stronger outcome.
back.direct: The deviation principle says: if the pre-cycle launch arrives at a position that would be actively contested after the cycle, the forced-march cost of incomplete preparation may be worth accepting. But the cost schedule is specific. What preparation is actually missing, and does its absence create a credibility problem at launch that would undermine the positional advantage gained by arriving before the cycle? A plan that arrives before the cycle but with credibility-damaging gaps has not executed the deviation. It has taken the forced march without the position.
back.competitive: The forced-march cost of launching before the cycle is real and specific: incomplete preparation means some fraction of the initiative's foundation does not arrive with the launch. The deviation analysis asks whether that cost is worth the positional advantage of arriving before the cycle. The correct analysis separates preparation into credibility-critical items that must be complete at launch and credibility-neutral items that can run in parallel. If the credibility-critical preparation can be completed before the cycle and the rest can travel alongside, the deviation works. If credibility-critical items remain incomplete, the forced march has been taken without the positional gain.

front.gentle: Tomas and Celia are deciding whether to launch before or after the quarterly planning cycle. Apply the deviation principle.
front.direct: Apply both the deviation principle and the forced-march cost schedule to Tomas and Celia's launch timing decision.
front.competitive: Diagnose Tomas and Celia's timing decision using the deviation principle and the forced-march cost framework. What is the correct analysis?

back.gentle: Baggage covers current capacity, provisions sustain daily survival, and supply bases enable the campaign to continue. Each converts the march into a sprint toward the edge of the army's effective range when lost. The army that outmarches its supply line has not extended its reach. It has eliminated its own reserve and is now racing against its own depletion.
back.direct: Baggage is current capacity: what the force can do right now. Provisions are daily survival: what keeps the march going. Supply bases are the ability to continue the campaign beyond the immediate march. Losing any one converts the march into a sprint toward the limit of the army's effective range. Each dependency is also a target the opponent can sever without engaging the force in direct combat.
back.competitive: Baggage, provisions, and supply bases form a chain in which the weakest link determines the campaign's effective range. Each dependency is simultaneously a planning constraint and an attack vector for a sophisticated opponent. An army that outmarches its supply line has not extended its reach. It has converted its campaign into a race against its own depletion, a race the opponent can win by simply waiting.

front.gentle: What are the three logistics dependencies Sun Tzu identifies, and why does losing any one of them end the campaign?
front.direct: State the three logistics dependencies and explain why each is both a planning constraint and a vulnerability the opponent can target.

back.gentle: The prohibition is against pursuing a retreating enemy that is simulating flight to bait an overextended pursuit. A competitor who is actually leaving a market is not baiting a pursuit.
